tokenization.intro: One sentence tokenized three ways: whole words, single characters, and subwords. Watch what happens to the word the vocabulary has never seen.

frames.headline: Splitting on spaces gives 4 tokens.
frames.detail: It's simple, but "unbelievable" isn't in the vocabulary, so it becomes [UNK] and its meaning is lost.

frames.headline: Characters never go unknown, but the same text costs 32 tokens.
frames.detail: Every letter is in a tiny vocabulary. The price is length: 8× the words, and attention cost grows with its square.

frames.headline: Subwords give 9 tokens and nothing is unknown.
frames.detail: "unbelievable" becomes un + believ + able, pieces the vocabulary already has. Common words stay whole; rare ones cost a few more.

frames.headline: The model never sees text, only these 9 ids.
frames.detail: Each id picks a row of the embedding table. The tokenizer is fixed before training, so this split is permanent.

bpe.intro: Four merge rounds learned from a tiny corpus, then those same merges replayed to encode a word the corpus never contained.

frames.headline: Start from single characters, so nothing is ever unknown.
frames.detail: The vocabulary is just the 11 symbols in the corpus. BPE's only question is how many pieces a word costs.

frames.headline: Round 1: "es" is the most frequent pair, 9 times.
frames.detail: Every adjacent pair is counted once per word, weighted by how often that word appears.

frames.headline: Merge "es" everywhere, adding exactly one token.
frames.detail: One merge, one new vocabulary entry: that is the only knob BPE turns.

frames.headline: Round 2: "est" is the most frequent pair, 9 times.
frames.detail: Every adjacent pair is counted once per word, weighted by how often that word appears.

frames.headline: Merge "est" everywhere, adding exactly one token.
frames.detail: One merge, one new vocabulary entry: that is the only knob BPE turns.

frames.headline: Round 3: "est</w>" is the most frequent pair, 9 times.
frames.detail: Every adjacent pair is counted once per word, weighted by how often that word appears.

frames.headline: Merge "est</w>" everywhere, adding exactly one token.
frames.detail: One merge, one new vocabulary entry: that is the only knob BPE turns.

frames.headline: Round 4: "lo" is the most frequent pair, 7 times.
frames.detail: Every adjacent pair is counted once per word, weighted by how often that word appears.

frames.headline: Merge "lo" everywhere, adding exactly one token.
frames.detail: One merge, one new vocabulary entry: that is the only knob BPE turns.

frames.headline: "lowest" never appeared in the corpus.
frames.detail: Encoding doesn't search for a split. It replays the learned merges, in the order they were learned.

frames.headline: Merge 1, e + s, applies to "lowest".
frames.detail: It reuses a piece learned from other words, which is how an unseen word still gets short.

frames.headline: Merge 2, es + t, applies to "lowest".
frames.detail: It reuses a piece learned from other words, which is how an unseen word still gets short.

frames.headline: Merge 3, est + </w>, applies to "lowest".
frames.detail: It reuses a piece learned from other words, which is how an unseen word still gets short.

frames.headline: Merge 4, l + o, applies to "lowest".
frames.detail: It reuses a piece learned from other words, which is how an unseen word still gets short.

frames.headline: "lowest" ends as 3 tokens, none unknown.
frames.detail: Frequent words collapse to one token and rare ones split. Sequence length then drives attention cost downstream.

hf_tokenizers.intro: BPE, WordPiece and Unigram trained on one corpus and compared on held-out text: how many pieces each needs, what happens to an unseen word, and what that costs a transformer.

frames.input: the gardener watched the smallest bird
frames.headline: BPE splits the held-out sentence into 10 tokens.
frames.detail: It replays the most frequent pair merges learned from the 15-sentence corpus.

frames.input: the gardener watched the smallest bird
frames.headline: WordPiece splits the held-out sentence into 10 tokens.
frames.detail: It merges the pair that most raises corpus likelihood, then encodes greedily from the left. "##" marks a piece that continues a word.

frames.input: the gardener watched the smallest bird
frames.headline: Unigram splits the held-out sentence into 9 tokens.
frames.detail: It starts from a large vocabulary, prunes it, then picks the most probable split with Viterbi.

rows.label: BPE
rows.value: u · n · b · e · l · i · e · v · a · b · l · e

rows.label: Unigram
rows.value: u · n · b · e · l · i · e · v · a · b · l · e

frames.headline: On an unseen word, WordPiece gives up with [UNK].
frames.detail: BPE falls back to characters and Unigram to its smallest pieces. Greedy longest-match has no fallback when nothing matches, which is why byte-level BPE has no [UNK] at all.

frames.input: the gardener watched the smallest bird
frames.method: compare at the same vocabulary size
frames.headline: Unigram needs the fewest pieces per word at the same vocabulary size.
frames.detail: Sequence length is attention cost: 10 pieces cost 100 pairwise scores and 9 cost 81, on every sequence for the life of the model.

frames.input: the gardener watched the smallest bird
frames.headline: Without a frequency floor, WordPiece spends its budget on one-off pairs.
frames.detail: Its score freq(ab)/(freq(a)·freq(b)) is highest when both halves occur once. A floor of 4 fixes it here; real trainers see billions of tokens.
